extracted.intended_audience: poets, creative writers, and students of poetic craft (readers of classical literary criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critical standards for composing and adapting poetry in the classical (Horatian) tradition: choices of subject, style, revision, suitability to audience and occasion, and practical conditions for composition. Emphasises taste, study, and matching task to ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy demands careful restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: "Tis thought that Comedy, drawing its themes from daily life, calls for less labour; but in truth it carries a heavier burden, as the indulgence allowed is less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic writing cannot rely on indulgence from the audience; because everyday subjects are expected to be handled well, the comic poet must take on a heavier burden of craftsmanship. Examples: Plautus' varied roles (young lover, close father, tricky pander) show skill in balancing character and audience expectation. Avoid cheap indulgences that court immediate laughter at the expense of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations must be worthy (vertere = transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you 'vertere' (not merely translate but transfer) Greek material to your stage, you must be able to 'digne vertere' — transfer it in worthy style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically translate foreign models; adapt only if you can render them suitably for your own audience and idiom. The text warns against attempting transfers in ignorance and advises pride in successful, dignified adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to delete — 'the art to blot'
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace (via commentator) cites that Dryden 'lacks the last and greatest art, the art to blot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision and ruthless cutting are essential skills of the poet. The ability to excise lines or passages that weaken the work is as important as compositional skill; cherish the discipline of pruning to improve overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to your capacity; avoid overreaching
rubrics_metrics.description: “neither does your majesty admit of a lowly strain, nor does my modesty dare to essay a task beyond my strength to bear.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose themes and tones you can conduct convincingly. Do not tackle grand subjects or a majestic strain unless you have the ability to sustain them; modesty in selecting subjects preserves dignity and prevents embarrassing misfit between subject and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine taste and careful diction are required
rubrics_metrics.description: “The writing of good poetry is a very serious matter, and demands a fine taste and careful discrimination in the choice of language.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for precision of word-choice, tonal appropriateness, and refined taste. What reads as 'ease' is often the result of much labour. Devote diligence to language selection rather than relying on facile effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seclusion and study are necessary for serious composition
rubrics_metrics.description: “How can I write poetry amid all the distractions of Rome? The poet must live in seclusion...” and praise of the man who gave seven years to study in Athens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious poetic work benefits from withdrawal and focused study; composing amid constant urban distractions (noise, errands, social calls) undermines the craft. The page contrasts quiet scholarly training with the chaos of public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the performance environment and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds, processions, chariots, exotic displays and other spectacles often drown the voice and distract audiences from the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for performance, be mindful that spectacle can overshadow voice and text. Anticipate noisy, distracted audiences; either adapt material to suit spectacle-heavy contexts or ensure that your dramatic devices can still register amid distraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not entrust great deeds to unworthy poets
rubrics_metrics.description: “What manner of ministers attend on Merit... never to be entrusted to an unworthy poet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great actions, leaders, or heroic themes deserve competent poetic treatment: poor verse can 'put a blot on bright exploits.' Select a poetial voice and level of craft commensurate with the subject's dignity (illustrated by Choerilus' cheapening of royal exploits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using verse to mask dishonourable acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace refuses 'to be praised in verses ill-thought' and rejects the idea of 'prave factis decorari versibus' (decorating bad deeds with verses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not employ poetry as mere flattery to conceal vice or ill conduct. Ethical integrity of content matters: the poet should not 'cleanse' or glorify wrongful acts by elegant phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that tastes vary; you cannot please all readers
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not all admire and love the same things... one rejoices in lyric, another in iambics, another in Bion's satiric style.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise diverse audience tastes and avoid trying to satisfy everyone. Choose your genre and intended readership rather than diluting work to chase universal approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence (sedulitas) rather than courting favour
rubrics_metrics.description: “Zeal is foolish to worry those it loves, above all when it commends itself by numbers and by art; for men more quickly learn and more gladly recall that which they deride than that which they approve and esteem.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work diligently on craft instead of seeking popularity or patronage through flattery. Careful art and disciplined composition earn lasting respect; ephemeral applause is unreliable and criticism sticks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful and accurate portrayal of characters and deeds
rubrics_metrics.description: “Features are seen with no more truth when moulded in statues of bronze, than are the manners and minds of famous heroes, when set forth in the poet's work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets bear responsibility for truthful rendering of personalities and historical actions. Strive for fidelity of character and situation so that poetic depiction reflects real moral and psychological texture.
